classification_signals: The abstract states: 'Based on experimental research with speculative research, and combining with examples, this paper addresses a series of issues about texture, including the concepts of and clarification between texture and perceived texture (texture perception); the dimensions of verbal description of texture; psychophysical relationship between subjective feelings of texture and physical parameters of materials; also addressed is the resources and inspirations from where texture can be generated.' (Page 2, Abstract)
The paper proposes definitions for 'texture' and 'perceived texture' (Page 5, Section 2).
It introduces a '{Dimension-lexicon} system' for material texture description (Page 5, Section 4).
It systematically classifies texture and discusses its generation sources, indicating a structured approach to understanding the concept.

While referring to 'experimental research' (Page 5, Section 4; Page 6, Section 5), the paper does not present detailed methods, results, or statistical analyses of these experiments, but rather uses them to support conceptual propositions.
title: Exploration into formal aesthetics in design: (material) texture

findings.consequent: Can include technological, functional, formal, psychological, and cultural aspects.
findings.quote: The connotation of aesthetics can include a number of aspects such as technological aesthetics, functional aesthetics, formal aesthetics, psychological and cultural aesthetics and so on.

findings.antecedent: Formal aesthetics (shape, colour, materials, texture, space, combination)
findings.consequent: Determines the 'styling' of any 3D product and environment.
findings.quote: Formal aesthetics concerning shape, colour, materials, texture, space etc (and of course their combination) is the fundamental target that designers should exclusively achieve, which radically/directly determines the 'styling' of any 3D product and environment.

findings.consequent: Less identified property; little understood how humans respond and perceive it.
findings.quote: Compared to colour, texture is a less identified property. Although an increasingly wide range of materials with abundant textures and surface effects are currently available in market, little has been understood about how human (both designers and users) respond and perceive them...

findings.antecedent: Understanding of how humans respond and perceive texture (physiologically and psychologically/culturally)
findings.consequent: Enables design practitioners to take into consideration rational thinking of texture creation and application.
findings.quote: This part of knowledge will enable design practitioners to take into consideration the rational thinking of texture creation and application as assistance to their innovative practice.
However, it is widely agreed that, in the first instance, aesthetic experience comes from the senses, or sensations [2], [3].

findings.antecedent: Formal elements (shape, colour, materials, texture, space, proportion, combination)
findings.consequent: Radically determine 'styling' of 3D products and significantly influence users' perception of beauty and value.
findings.quote: These formal elements radically determine the ‘styling' of any 3D products and significantly influences users' perception of the product's beauty and value.

findings.consequent: More ambiguous and difficult to identify.
findings.quote: Compared with the properties of colour, sound etc, texture seems to be a property that is more ambiguous and difficult to identify.

findings.consequent: Defined as 'the geometrical configuration and physical-chemical attributes of surface or bulk of materials/objects'.
findings.quote: We propose to define 'texture' as 'the geometrical configuration and physical-chemical attributes of surface or bulk of materials/objects'.

findings.consequent: Defined as 'a synthesis of physiological and psychological response and impression to the geometrical configuration and physical-chemical attributes of the surface or the bulk of materials/objects'.
findings.quote: Correspondingly, we propose a definition of perceived texture as 'a synthesis of physiological and psychological response and impression to the geometrical configuration and physical-chemical attributes of the surface or the bulk of materials/objects'.

findings.antecedent: Correlation between objective texture attributes (physical parameters) and subjective texture perception
findings.consequent: Provides framework for creating suitable, aesthetic material textures.
findings.quote: The understanding of the correlation between the objective texture attributes (usually represented by physical parameters) and the subjective texture perception will provide the framework for creating suitable, aesthetic material textures.

findings.consequent: Proposed a {Dimension-lexicon} system to summarise material texture description into geometrical, physical-chemical, emotional, and associative dimensions.
findings.quote: From our experimental research, a {Dimension-lexicon} system [12] has been proposed to summarise the material texture description.

findings.antecedent: Sensory modality (visual touch vs. blindfolded touch)
findings.consequent: Subjects' sensitivity to emotional feelings (e.g., comfortable – uncomfortable) when touching material surfaces.
findings.quote: Subjects seem to be more sensitive to the emotional feelings under the visual touch conditions. However, when blindfolded, subjects are still equally sensitive to the feeling of comfort comfortable – uncomfortable when touching the material surface [12].

findings.antecedent: Understanding relationships between objective parameters (e.g., roughness, hardness) and subjective feelings of texture
findings.consequent: Helps identify technical aspects of texture selection and pinpoint processes for suitable parameters, maximizing positive user feelings.
findings.quote: Understanding the relationships between the objective parameters and subjective responses will help to further identify the technical aspects of texture selection, to pinpoint particular technical processes for materials and surfaces with suitable parameters, which correspond to the maximising mixture of positive user feelings.
The relationship between physical roughness and psychological roughness tends to conform to a power law [7] [14].

findings.consequent: Psychological feeling of a surface's moisture.
findings.quote: people's psychological feeling of a surface's moisture could be related to a number of physical factors, such as different materials with different surface energy...

findings.antecedent: Different materials with different surface roughness or softness (for the same material type)
findings.consequent: Psychological feeling of a surface's moisture.
findings.quote: ...or the same type of materials with different surface roughness, or the same type of materials but with different softness [11].

findings.consequent: A number of psychological feelings (e.g., subjective roughness, stickiness, warmth).
findings.quote: On the other hand, one physical parameter, e.g. the physical roughness, can correspond to a number of psychological feelings, e.g. subjective roughness, stickiness, warmth.

findings.consequent: Can be generated or learnt from nature, mind & fantasy, innovation in science & technology, virtual reality, micro-world, and social events.
findings.quote: Texture can be generated or learnt from nature, mind & fantasy, innovation in science & technology, virtual reality, micro-world and social events.

limitations: Little has been understood about how human (both designers and users) respond and perceive textures, either physiologically or psychologically and culturally.
There is a lack of a systematic classification for texture description, with character dimensions varying between researchers.
minimum_safe_summary: This paper explores formal aesthetics in design, focusing on material texture. It proposes definitions for objective 'texture' and subjective 'perceived texture', outlining a {Dimension-lexicon} system for describing texture across geometrical, physical-chemical, emotional, and associative dimensions. The authors discuss the psychophysical relationships between objective material parameters (like roughness) and subjective human responses, noting that understanding these correlations can aid in creating aesthetic textures. They also identify various sources for texture generation, including nature, fantasy, virtual reality, technological advancements, the micro-world, and social events. A key limitation is the current lack of systematic understanding and classification of how humans perceive and respond to texture.
